newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: BRIBERY THREAT STAYS ALIVE IN ASIAN SOCCER.
newsitem.headline: BRIBERY THREAT STAYS ALIVE IN ASIAN SOCCER.

text.p: Match-fixing in Asian soccer is under control after a crackdown by football bodies and governments in the region, but complacency could allow the menace to return, Asia's top soccer official said.
"By no means we feel the corruption has come to an end," Peter Velappan, secretary-general of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), told Reuters. "It's only on hold now."

The AFC, headquartered in Malaysia, moved two years ago to check bribery in regional soccer after stumbling on a Malaysian-based syndicate trying to fix matches in Britain with the alleged help of former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar.

At the height of the clampdown, some 102 Malaysian football players, bookies, coaches and even officials, were arrested for match-fixing. Seventy-two were banned for life from the game, while about a dozen were put under restricted residence under the country's tough Internal Security Act, which permits detentions of up to two years without trial.
The Malaysian action, followed up in Singapore, forced betting syndicates to lie low in most parts of the region, said Velappan.
"There was a lot of dispute about the methods used by authorities, but it was the best thing to do," he said. "The corruption had got so bad that we were exporting it to Britain."
Grobbelaar now faces trial in London on charges on rigging games with former Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers, ex-Wimbledon and Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim.
Vellapan said the vigilance against match-fixing should continue in Asia as its threat to the game remained.

"We can nab the bookies but we can never get enough evidence to touch the syndicates," Velappan said. "The syndicates are very much alive and they're into everything from horse racing to all other games."
The AFC was now trying to mould a "new generation of young players who would learn from the faults of the older ones", Velappan said.

"Gambling is part of life in Asia and syndicates pick on a player from the time he's in a small club, so that by the time he enters the world scene, he'd be totally under their control," said Velappan.
"So we're telling the youngsters -- don't let greed spoil a beautiful game."
He said part of the corrective action was to make football more rewarding for the region's players, who often complain of getting too little money from the game.
"In West Asia, match-fixing is almost non-existent as the players are paid well," Velappan said.

"As far as Southeast Asian players are concerned, those in Malaysia and Singapore should have no excuse as they get more than they deserve. But we certainly have a problem with economies like Indonesia and Thailand."
